text: Understanding Drug Addiction: Implications for Treatment ALAN. LESHNER National Institute on Drug Abuse The addicted brain is qualitatively different from the nonaddicted brain, in ways that include glucose use, gene expression, and responsiveness to environmental cues. Such discoveries place researchers in the early but hopeful stages of translating fundamental, findings into new treatments that address the neurobiologic basis of drug craving—even for cocaine, against which there are currently no pharmacologic interventions. Drug addiction is fundamentally a brain disease. This seemingly straightforward observation is ac- tually the outcome of dramatic changes in our un- derstanding of substance abuse. Before the ad- vances, addiction was typically seen as a purely be- havioral disorder, characterized internally by drug ‘craving and externally by compulsive {and harm- ful) drug-seeking behavior. Its chtef pathophysio- logic manifestation was the withdrawal syndrome resulting from abstinence. Neurobiologically, how- ‘ever, it is now known that the drug-addicted brain is qualitatively different from the nonaddicted. brain, as manifested, for example. by global de- lines in glucose metabolism and intraneuronal ‘changes in gene expression. In effect. a “switch” has ‘been thrown, Although the precise molecular na- ture of the swith remains unknown, current knowledge implicates activation of the brain's mesolimbic dopamine system as a common de- ‘nominator in atleast the acute effects of all abused rugs, Behavioral-science advances have been equally significant. They show that the addicted brain ts abnormally conditioned, so that environmental ‘cues surrounding druguse have become partof the addiction. Suspicion of the importance of such ‘cues dates at least to the era of the Vietnam Wer. from which roughly 100.000 Americans returned addicted to heroin, In the United States, these per- sons often overcame their addiction with much less distress than 1s typically the case for American street addicts. The crucial difference appears to have been that the military personnel returned to an environment completely different from the one in which their addiction developed. Both lines of investigation have implications for Ce ha cen Carpanas ne Bers tern treatment. The neurobiologic advances represent initial efforts to identify the changes induced by chronic substance abuse. and thus to address the physical basis of drug craving, Specific pharmaco- logic intervention would aim to throw the addiction switch back. Meanwhile, the behavioral-science ‘advances emphasize that drug addiction ts a brain disease embedded in a social context. Treatment must therefore include deconditioning to extin- guish cues that would otherwise be inducements for relapse. Together, the ines of research point to- ‘ward eventual treatment programs more compre- hensive and more effective than those we currently have. The Emerging Neurobiology Among the wealth of findings that now illuminate the basis of drug addiction in the brain, the most ‘elemental, but critical, has been the identification of the molecular sites of action for every major abused drug. Each such drug affects a particular ‘set of cell-surface receptors. transmembrane ion ‘channels, or transmembrane transporter (pump) molecules. For example. opiates bind to the brain's opioid receptors, whereas cocaine binds to the ‘pump molecule responsible for uptake of the neu- rotransmitter dopamine into presynaptic axon ter- minals. To this extent. each abused drug affects its own brain system, establishing the individuality of ach such substance—n individuality distinguish- able to drug abusers. Dr. Leshner is Director. To the Editor.—We were very interested in the JAMIA Medi- cal News & Perspectives* article on mammography and the comments of Naney Breen, PhD. She states that “[olne of the problems is that the women who need screening most—older women are at higher risk for breast cancer—often are using a cardiologist or other physician who is treating their main disease as their source of primary care. But those physicians do not think of themselves as primary care doctors, so they donot recommend or ask ifthe woman has had a mammogram this year.” However, the article cited by Breen and Kessler provides no supporting data for this view. ‘One of us (8.8.8. isa thyroidologist who had not previously screened patients with mammography. In an initial study, we compared the mammogram results obtained during a 6-month period of 75 patients with thyroid disease from the subspe- tialist’s thyroid practice with those of 57 eontrols without thyroid disease from a general internist’s practice. The mean (SD) age of the patients with thyroid disease was 53.16 (12.9) years as opposed to 64.36 (19.7) years for the eontrol group. {P<.001). We were concerned when three new breast cancers were discovered among the patients with thyroid disease Gubspecialist practice), whereas no new breast cancers were found in the patients from the general internal medicine practice population. In retrospect, we feel that this was be- cause of a selection bias. Only 18% of the patients in the general internist population had not had previous mammo- ‘grams, whereas 64% of the patients in the subspecialist popu- lation had no previous mammography In a subsequent retrospective study, 1000 conseeutive pa- tients with thyroid disease in the subspecialist practice were found to have 33 breast eancers (8.8%). In 228 control patients without thyroid disease obtained from general internal medi cine practices, there were 12 breast cancers (5.4%) (P<.008). ‘The mean (SD) age of the patients with thyroid disease was 478 (15.8) years, whereas the mean age of the control group was 60.7 (17.6) years (P<.001). The average age of breast eancer onset in the thyroid group was 56.5 (12.1) years as ‘opposed to 57.1 (18.9) years in the control group (P>.55). Of the 88 breast caneer patients in the thyroid population, 11 (83%) were not taking levothyroxine at the onset of breast cancer. Their mean (SD) age was 58.5 (1.7) years (P>.25) when compared with controls). The average age of breast cancer onset of the remaining 22 patients (67%) receiving Ievothyroxine was 58.0 (12.9) years (P>.5 when compared with controls). There were 189 patients with a history of therapy with radioactive iodine (180 for hyperthyroidism and nine for thyroid cancer treatment). Only four of these had breast cancer 2.1%). ‘We concluded that neither thyroid disease nor thyroid supplementation increased the risk of breast cancer in the lied. Physician subspecialists who do not normally cancer should make an effort to ensure that their patients ave being adequately screened, if not by them- selves, then at least by other physicians. The subspecialist may be the only physician the patient ever sees. Such an effort might result in identifying an increased number of early breast cancers. Sheldon S. Stoffer, MD 'E. And we ate ap- lled by what the lay press has done cautious and unexceptionable re- marks, Dr. Little reviews the experimental studies supported by the Council's grants testing whether “tobacco smoke might hhave activity as a direct-contact car- cinogen.” He concludes: “The over-all. impres- sion gained from these many bioassay studies is that tobacco smoke is active or of extremely minute activity in these several artificial systems, none of which of course actually measures hu- ‘man response under realistic conditions. ‘The results lend litle 10 support the hy- pothesis that cigarette smoke can act 25 8 direct-contact carcinogen in the human lung. Study is continuing with respect 10 fother hypothetical modes of action.” ‘The experimental systems used for bioassay of tobacco smoke and its con- densates are indeed artificial, and one is surely entitled to question their support ‘of a “hypothesis that cigarette smoke can act as a direct-contact carcinogen in the bbumarr lung such ‘Suudy” or “Report by Tobacco Council Finds No Cigarette Link to Cancer,” and the stories tha to support’, the charge that cigarette smoke produces cancer” are a far cry from Dr. Litle’s careful statement He does, however, state: “Lung can- cer is a rare disease.” Well, how rare is rare? Cancer as an entity is the second ‘cause of death in this country. In 1962, deaths attributed to all cancer causes totaled 278,562. In that same year, deaths from lung. cancer numbered 41,376, A very rapid calculation shows that one out of seven cancer deaths was due to lung cancer. Is this rare? Dr. Little also makes much of the fol- lowing: “Although the actual number of deaths from lung cancer is increasing be- cause of population growth and because of larger numbers of persons in the high age groups, the rate of increase in the age-corrected death rate has been slowing down since 1930. This declining rate of increase, viewed in the light of actual and per capita consumption of cigarettes during this period, raises a serious ques- tion concerning the validity of the simple causation theory and demonstrates. the ‘eed for continued study and observation,’ ‘There was about a ninefold increase in the age-adjusted mortality for cancer ff the lung between 1930 and 1960. A casual glance at tables of vital statisti suggests that if the reported rate of. in- crease between 1930 and 1935 had con- tinued as such for the next 25 years, then the mortality for cancer of the lung in 1960 would have been about 11 or 12 times that of 1930, Dr. Little seems to be saying that this “rare disease,” which has demonstrated a remarkable increase in mortality, ought to be increasing even ‘more rapidly if there is any simple cau sality relationship to cigarette smoking, Why this should be so is quite unclear. ‘We do not believe that Dr, Little's re- Port is in any way reassuring to smokers Te does not invalidate the conclusions reached by the Surgeon General's Advis- ‘ory Committee.
